units.title: What is an AP?
units.key_idea: An arithmetic progression is a list of numbers where you add the same number (the common difference d) each time.
units.body:
Priya saves ₹50 in the first week, ₹60 in the second, ₹70 in the third, and so on. Her savings each week form the list:
50, 60, 70, 80, ...

Each number is 10 more than the one before. A list like this, where we add the same fixed number every time, is called an arithmetic progression (AP).

• The first term is called a. Here a = 50.
• The fixed number added each time is the common difference d. Here d = 10.

To find d, subtract any term from the next one: d = 60 − 50 = 10.

d can be:
• positive: 3, 7, 11, 15 ... (d = 4)
• negative: 20, 17, 14, 11 ... (d = −3), like water in a tank going down by the same amount each day
• zero: 5, 5, 5, 5 ... (d = 0)

Not every list is an AP. 1, 2, 4, 8 ... is not an AP because the differences are 1, 2, 4, which are not the same.

units.title: The nth term
units.key_idea: The nth term of an AP is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
units.body:
We don't need to write the whole list to find a far-away term. There is a formula.

Think about it: to reach the 2nd term, you add d once. To reach the 3rd, you add d twice. To reach the nth term, you add d (n − 1) times. So:

aₙ = a + (n − 1)d

Example 1: Priya saves 50, 60, 70, ... How much does she save in week 12?
a = 50, d = 10, n = 12.
a₁₂ = 50 + (12 − 1) × 10 = 50 + 110 = ₹160.

Example 2: Which term of the AP 3, 8, 13, 18, ... is 78?
a = 3, d = 5. We want aₙ = 78.
78 = 3 + (n − 1) × 5
75 = (n − 1) × 5
n − 1 = 15 → n = 16. So 78 is the 16th term.

Example 3: A tree is 1.2 m tall and grows 0.3 m every year. Its height in the 5th year is 1.2 + 4 × 0.3 = 2.4 m.

units.title: Sum of an AP
units.key_idea: The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], or n/2 × (first term + last term).
units.body:
How much does Priya save in total in 10 weeks if she saves 50, 60, 70, ...?

There is a neat trick. Write the sum forwards and backwards:
S = 50 + 60 + ... + 140
S = 140 + 130 + ... + 50
Add them: every pair adds to 190, and there are 10 pairs. So 2S = 10 × 190, and S = 950.

This gives the formulas:
Sₙ = n/2 × (first term + last term)
Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example 1: Sum of the first 10 terms of 50, 60, 70, ...
S₁₀ = 10/2 × [2 × 50 + 9 × 10] = 5 × [100 + 90] = 5 × 190 = ₹950.

Example 2: Sum of the first 100 natural numbers, 1 + 2 + ... + 100:
S = 100/2 × (1 + 100) = 50 × 101 = 5050.

Example 3: Logs are stacked with 20 in the bottom row, 19 in the next, down to 5 at the top. There are 16 rows. Total = 16/2 × (20 + 5) = 8 × 25 = 200 logs.

units.title: Sides of a right triangle
units.key_idea: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; the other sides are named 'opposite' and 'adjacent' from the chosen angle.
units.body:
Trigonometry studies the relation between the sides and angles of a triangle. We start with a right triangle: one angle is exactly 90°.

Imagine a ladder leaning against a house wall. The wall, the ground and the ladder form a right triangle. The right angle is where the wall meets the ground.

Naming the sides:
1. Hypotenuse: the longest side, opposite the right angle. Here it is the ladder.
2. Pick the angle between the ladder and the ground; call it θ (theta).
3. Opposite side: the side facing θ. Here it is the wall height.
4. Adjacent side: the side next to θ that is not the hypotenuse. Here it is the ground distance from the wall.

If we pick the other angle (at the top of the ladder), the opposite and adjacent sides swap. The hypotenuse never changes.

The sides follow Pythagoras' theorem:
Hypotenuse² = Opposite² + Adjacent²
If the wall height is 4 m and the ladder's foot is 3 m from the wall, the ladder is √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5 m long.

units.title: sin, cos and tan
units.key_idea: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
units.body:
For an angle θ in a right triangle, we define three ratios:

• sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse
• cos θ = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse
• tan θ = Opposite ÷ Adjacent

A memory trick: "Some People Have Curly Brown Hair Through Proper Brushing" gives S = P/H, C = B/H, T = P/B, where P is perpendicular (opposite), B is base (adjacent) and H is hypotenuse.

Example: the ladder triangle with opposite = 4, adjacent = 3, hypotenuse = 5.
sin θ = 4/5, cos θ = 3/5, tan θ = 4/3.

These ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle. A small 3-4-5 triangle and a big 6-8-10 triangle have the same angles and the same ratios.

Useful facts:
1. tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.
2. sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (from Pythagoras). Check: (4/5)² + (3/5)² = 16/25 + 9/25 = 1. ✓
3. Because the hypotenuse is the longest side, sin θ and cos θ are never more than 1.

units.title: Using trigonometry: heights
units.key_idea: Using tan θ = height ÷ distance, you can find the height of a tree or tower without climbing it.
units.body:
Trigonometry lets us measure heights we cannot climb.

Standing on the ground, if you look up at the top of a tree, your line of sight makes an angle with the ground. This is the angle of elevation.

Some standard values (remember these):
• tan 45° = 1
• tan 30° = 1/√3 ≈ 0.58
• tan 60° = √3 ≈ 1.73
• sin 30° = 1/2, cos 60° = 1/2

Example 1: You stand 20 m from a tree. The angle of elevation of its top is 45°.
tan 45° = height ÷ 20 → 1 = height ÷ 20 → height = 20 m.

Example 2: A water tank tower casts a shadow 10 m long when the sun's elevation is 60°.
tan 60° = height ÷ 10 → height = 10 × √3 ≈ 17.3 m.

Example 3: A 10 m ladder makes a 60° angle with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
sin 60° = height ÷ 10, and sin 60° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87, so height ≈ 8.7 m.

Safety: when using a ladder, keep its base firm and ask someone to hold it.
